newsitem.title: UK: London precious metals biased to downside.
newsitem.headline: London precious metals biased to downside.

text.p: The precious metals market was gingerly testing its bottom levels on Monday after recent tumbles to fresh lows, dealers and analysts said.
But a short-term stabilisation would not eliminate the risk of more losses in coming days, with weakened silver dragging gold and the other precious metals lower, they added.
"I think everyone's looking for the bottom in this market but no one has the courage to call it," a dealer said.
"After we've seen the markets come off we should look to consolidate and see a bit of a bounce," he added.
But big U.S. investment funds, which have been driving the sell-off in silver and other metals since last week may want to keep pushing prices lower, he added.
"We haven't seen a big breakdown yet," the dealer said
Bullion was trading at 2-1/2 month lows and fixed at $381.20 an ounce, compared to $381.75 on Friday afternoon.
Gold's hold on a historical support level just under $380 was tenuous but holding for now, analysts said.

"The decline is slowing enough so that support of this critical nature is likely to hold. But I don't think it will longer term," said technical analyst Elli Gifford of Investment Research of Cambridge.
"If we're going to see a major move in gold at all, then it will be down," she said.
Silver, currently at 18-month lows, was barely changed from Friday's weaker London close at $4.88 an ounce. But a test of potential buying interest at $4.80 was expected eventually.
"The picture in silver has deteriorated, and although I think support below $4.80 will hold for now, I don't think it's got much in the way of upside scope right now," Gifford said.
Platinum continued to feel the heat from silver's weakness, fixing at a fresh near 2-1/2 year low of $386.50 an ounce.
The platinum group metals were also still under pressure from steady Russian supplies and sluggish demand from the Japanese electronics industry.
Palladium was also weaker, down $1.00 from Friday's close at $118.75 an ounce. Its slide last week below $120 support left it vulnerable to dipping into the $112-$115 area, dealers said.
